source.title: Latent Adversarial Training Improves Robustness to Persistent Harmful Behaviors in LLMs
source.authors: A. Sheshadri; Aidan Ewart; Phillip Guo; Aengus Lynch; Cindy Wu; V. Hebbar; Henry Sleight; Asa Cooper Stickland; Ethan Perez; Dylan Hadfield-Menell; Stephen Casper

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates harmful-completion success under several jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, on refusal-trained models. It uses different methods and measures from the claim’s original studies and does not analyze first-token KL concentration.
record.gate_note: The jailbreak evaluations in Table 2 and the alternate-autograder evaluation in Table 7 report attack-success outcomes relevant to V4. Training and unlearning results elsewhere in the paper do not test the listed fine-tuning-erosion or safety-localization versions. The paper does not measure per-token KL or test suffixes or decoding changes.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper (targeted LAT), but Table 2 and Table 7 report attack success on the undefended chat models and on refusal-retrained (RT) models. Prefilling and suffix-optimisation attacks (AutoPrompt, GCG, Many-Shot+GCG) are among the attacks, so these rates bear on V4 in a new setting with different graders. Nothing in the paper tests V1–V3, V5 or V6. LAT perturbs prompt positions only and is not framed as deepening safety beyond the first tokens, so V7 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that targeted LAT augments refusal training, outperforming R2D2 with far less compute, and that manual red-teaming still jailbroke their Llama3 LAT model. The paraphrase omits that they also claim LAT improves backdoor removal and robust unlearning, including resistance to re-learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models with refusal training and latent adversarial perturbations, then measures jailbreak attack success; it does not reproduce the original harmful- or benign-fine-tuning interventions or token-position KL analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack method, defense method, model, and autograder change the reported attack-success rates. The paper reports that StrongReject may produce false positives and that HarmBench classifies more attacks as successful.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted LAT on prompt-position latents lowers prefill ASR (Llama3 0.135→0.068 SR; Llama2 0.106→0.029). Untargeted LAT raises Llama3 prefill ASR to 0.375 (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Latent adversarial training restricted to prompt positions improves robustness to prefilling attacks; the gain depends on targeting the adversary toward harmful completions.

record.problems: Jailbreak success uses automated graders; the authors estimate that in some cases a majority of StrongReject-labeled successes may be false positives. Reported means use n = 3 random seeds. Experiments are limited to models with fewer than 10 billion parameters.
record.rows_left_out: None of the Table 2 jailbreak attack-success outcomes were left out. From Appendix D, Table 7, only prefilling outcomes were extracted; the other attack outcomes under the alternate HarmBench judge were omitted to keep the record focused on the directly relevant prefilling condition.

untested.parts: Decoding changes are not tested. The paper does not show that attacks work by getting past the opening tokens, and gives no per-position analysis.
Not tested. The only few-shot fine-tuning attacks are on unlearned knowledge (WMDP), not on refusal.
Not tested. LAT is not a depth-of-alignment method.

missing.what: Attack success on the undefended Llama2-7B-chat and Llama3-8B-instruct (direct, prefill, AutoPrompt, GCG, Many-Shot). This is the cleanest V4 evidence; e.g. prefill 0.277/0.488 under StrongReject.
missing.locator: Table 2, unlabelled first row per model

missing.what: Undefended-model attack success under the HarmBench grader (Llama2 prefill about 0.594, GCG 0.417, many-shot 0.949; Llama3 prefill about 0.729)
HarmBench-grader GCG/AutoPrompt/Many-Shot rows for RT models (e.g. Llama2 RT GCG 0.490, many-shot 0.458)

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly a defense paper, and its V4 relevance is incidental. Undefended-model values were read from garbled table text, so column alignment is uncertain; verify against the PDF. The authors warn that StrongReject may give a majority of false positives in some cases.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples as a cause of safety loss.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning as a cause of increased harmful compliance.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Tests prefilling and several jailbreak attacks, but not suffixes or decoding changes; does not establish that attacks work by getting past the first response tokens.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or the training objective causes first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate safety spread beyond the first tokens.

relationships.condition: Undefended Llama2-7B-chat and Llama3-8B-instruct, prefilling and GCG/AutoPrompt suffix attacks
relationships.reason: Based on the text, because no row records this. As read from the garbled tables: Llama2 prefill ASR 0.277 vs direct 0.000 (StrongReject), 0.594 (HarmBench); Llama3 prefill 0.488 vs direct about 0.086. GCG is about 0.2.
relationships.display_finding: In approximate table readings, Llama2 prefill ASR was 0.277 against 0.000 direct on StrongReject and 0.594 on HarmBench, Llama3 prefill was 0.488 against about 0.086 direct, and GCG was about 0.2.

relationships.condition: Models given additional refusal training (RT); StrongReject vs HarmBench grader
relationships.reason: After RT, prefill and suffix attacks reach only 0.01–0.23 ASR, far from defeating refusal. Rates also roughly double under HarmBench vs StrongReject (T2-L2-RT-PREFILL, T2-L3-RT-PREFILL, T2-L2-RT-GCG, T2-L3-RT-AUTOPROMPT, T2-L2-RT-PREFILL-HB, T2-L3-RT-PREFILL-HB).
relationships.display_finding: After refusal training, prefill and suffix attacks reached only 0.01–0.23 attack success. Rates roughly doubled under the HarmBench grader compared with StrongReject.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Prefilling and other jailbreak attacks on refusal-trained RT models, under StrongReject and HarmBench
reader_labels.reason: Successful harmful completions are reported for prefilling and several other attacks on RT models; the prefilling rates are nonzero in both model families and both graders (rows T2-L2-RT-PREFILL, T2-L3-RT-PREFILL, T2-L2-RT-PREFILL-HB, T2-L3-RT-PREFILL-HB). These results support vulnerability to the tested attacks, but do not establish the proposed first-token mechanism.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LAT-augmented defenses and several other defense/attack combinations
reader_labels.reason: Attack success is often low or zero, and LAT reduces prefilling success relative to RT in the reported comparisons; thus the tested attacks do not invariably defeat refusal (rows T2-L2-LAT-PREFILL, T2-L3-LAT-PREFILL, T2-L2-LAT-PREFILL-HB, T2-L3-LAT-PREFILL-HB).
